claim: Pabitra Krishna Bhattacharya was affiliated with the Department of Chemistry at M.S. University of Baroda.
Bhattacharya retired as Professor and Head of that department in 2001 after 34 years of service.
He obtained MSc and PhD degrees from the University of Saugor, Madhya Pradesh.
He held a Fulbright-Hays senior fellowship at Ohio State University during 1976–1977.
His stated research interests included coordination chemistry, bioinorganic chemistry, and homogeneous catalysis.
Bhattacharya and B. T. Thaker published a 1979 study of mixed-ligand Schiff-base complexes of copper(II) and nickel(II).
Bhattacharya and V. K. Patel determined formation constants for ternary copper systems in 1:1 dioxane-water at 30 °C in a 1985 study of catecholate-ring substitution.

A 1985 paper by Bhattacharya, P. J. Patel, and V. K. Patel compared ternary nickel-complex stability with corresponding copper complexes while investigating a proposed metalloenzyme-selection question.
A 1989 paper coauthored by Bhattacharya reported alkene epoxidation by mono- and binuclear iron(III) Schiff-base chelates using iodosylbenzene.
The 1989 study reported that its binuclear complexes performed better than the mononuclear complexes for norbornene epoxidation.
Bhattacharya published a 1990 paper specifically on homogeneous olefin-epoxidation catalysis by mono- and binuclear Schiff-base complexes.
The 2020 second edition of Metal Ions in Biochemistry lists Pabitra Krishna Bhattacharya and Prakash B. Samnani as authors.
A publisher author biography reports that 37 students obtained PhDs under Bhattacharya's supervision.

By 2001, the scientific literature described several enzymes as nickel-dependent, so the premise in the title of Bhattacharya's 1985 nickel paper must be read as a historical research question rather than a current general fact.
Bhattacharya's paper trail connects solution coordination thermodynamics, bioinorganic questions, and biomimetic homogeneous catalysis.
This body of work is relevant to modern catalyst design because ligand architecture and nuclearity are variables used to tune metal-complex reactivity.
The 1990 paper reported oxidation of various olefins using Mn(III) Schiff-base complexes and binuclear Mn(II) and Fe(III) Schiff-base complexes as catalysts.
The 1990 paper correlated catalytic activity with ligand structure, metal-ion redox potential, and the binuclear character of the complex.
